transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic? What's been concerning you?

Hi, doctor. Thank you for seeing me. 

Well, I came in because I'm just having a really hard time stopping my thoughts. Once a worry starts—whether it's about my mother getting up at night, or a grant report, or just wondering if I missed something at work—I just can't seem to shelve it in my mind. I try. I make lists, I try really hard to redirect myself to something else, but it doesn't work. I just can't seem to stop the worrying once it gets going.

When these thoughts come to you—like about your mother or the grant report—do they feel like they're coming from your own mind, or do they sometimes feel like they're being forced into your head against your will?

No, they definitely feel like my own thoughts. It's not like someone else is putting them there or anything like that. It's just my own brain going into overdrive and getting stuck on things I need to do or things I'm afraid might happen.

Besides worries about your mother, the grant report, and work, are there other areas of your life where you find yourself worrying a lot—like your health, finances, relationships, or things in general? And how long have you been experiencing this pattern of constant worry?

Well, it's been going on for about a year now. Over this past year, it feels like the worrying has just... spread. It started out mostly being about my mother’s safety, but now it's about finances, staff decisions I have to make, deadlines, the house... and just whether I’m being a good daughter in general. It's gotten to the point where even really small things can start to feel like they’re about to completely unravel.

When you're experiencing this worry and difficulty stopping your thoughts, do you notice any physical symptoms—like feeling restless or tense, trouble sleeping, getting tired easily, or having trouble concentrating on tasks?

Yes, I definitely get tense. Um, by the end of the day, my neck and shoulders just feel completely locked up from bracing myself all the time. And I actually catch myself clenching my jaw a lot, too—especially when I'm answering emails or just sitting there listening for my mother in the next room.
How much is this constant worrying interfering with your ability to do your job, take care of your mother, or enjoy things you normally would? Is it causing you significant distress?

It is definitely causing me a lot of distress, especially at work. Um, at the library, I’ve started missing these small but really important details. That is just not like me at all. It actually got bad enough recently that I had to hand off parts of a grant presentation to a colleague because I just... I froze. It's honestly making me worry a lot about whether I can keep leading my team well when I'm struggling to get through things like that. So, yes, it's definitely interfering with my day-to-day life.

Have you ever experienced sudden episodes where your anxiety or worry suddenly spikes very intensely—where your heart races, you feel like you can't breathe, or you feel like something terrible is about to happen right now, even if there's no immediate threat?

No, I don't think I've ever had anything like that. The worry is just... always there, kind of humming in the background all day. But it doesn't suddenly spike or make me feel like I can't breathe or anything like that. It's more of a constant, exhausting feeling than a sudden attack.

When you're worrying about these things—like your mother's safety or work deadlines—do you recognize that you might be worrying more than the situation really warrants, or does the worry feel completely justified and proportional to what could actually happen?

Um... I'm really not sure how to answer that. When I'm worrying, it... it feels completely justified to me. Like, of course I need to worry about my mom falling or messing up the grant. It feels very real in the moment. 

I don't know if I'm worrying more than the situation warrants. I guess I haven't really thought about it that way. It just feels like these are things I absolutely have to stay on top of, or something bad will happen.

Looking back on situations where you were worried—like about your mother or work—have there been times afterward when you realized that what you were worried about either didn't happen, or turned out to be much less serious than you feared?

Um, I guess... I mean, yes, there are definitely times where things turn out fine. Like, I'll worry all week about a deadline at the library, and then we meet it without any major disasters. Or I'll be convinced my mom is going to slip in the bathroom, and she doesn't. 

But even when nothing bad happens, it doesn't really stop the worry for the next time. It's not like I look back and think, "Oh, I was being silly." It just feels like we got lucky that time, you know? The worry just shifts to the next thing right away.

Besides trying to redirect your thoughts or making lists, do you find yourself doing any specific repetitive actions or rituals—like checking things multiple times, arranging things in a certain way, or doing things in a particular order—to try to manage or reduce your worry?

No, I don't really do anything like that. I don't have rituals or feel the need to arrange things in a certain way. And I don't check things over and over. I mean, I might double-check a list to make sure I didn't forget something for work, but not in a repetitive, ritualistic way. It's really just the constant thinking and worrying, not so much doing physical actions to try and stop it.
